text: Why does Java check array bounds on every access, given the cost?
choices: Because bounds checking is required to support garbage collection of arrays.
Because the alternative is reading or writing memory outside the array, which is the mechanism behind decades of buffer-overflow vulnerabilities.
Because without it, array indices could not be computed from user input safely.
Because the JVM cannot determine array lengths at compile time, unlike C.
explanation: The cost is real and the JIT eliminates much of it by proving indices in range for simple loops. What you buy is that an out-of-range index becomes an exception naming the index and the length, rather than a silent read of adjacent memory. Chapter 15 cites the vulnerability histories directly: this is one of the clearest cases in the book where a language's safety decision has a measurable effect on the world.
